stem.en: Quick recall before we start: a book rests on a table, not moving. Which statement correctly describes the forces acting on it?

text.en: Gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up with an equal, opposite force — the two forces balance to a net force of zero.

feedback.en: Right — two real forces are acting, they just happen to cancel. 'Not moving' means net force zero, not 'no forces at all.'

text.en: No forces act on the book at all — that's why it isn't moving.

feedback.en: A very common mix-up: 'not moving' does NOT mean 'no forces.' Gravity is definitely pulling the book down right now — something else must be holding it up, or it would fall.

text.en: Only gravity acts on it; the table just 'holds it in place' without pushing on it.

feedback.en: If only gravity acted, the book would accelerate downward — it doesn't, so something must be pushing back. The table surface genuinely exerts an upward force; it isn't a passive, force-free 'holder.'

explanation.en: This is the idea this lesson builds on directly: a net force of zero — not an absence of forces — is what leaves an object's velocity unchanged, whether that velocity is zero (at rest) or some constant nonzero value (cruising).

hints.en: If gravity is the only force acting, what would happen to the book? Does that match what you actually see?
Two forces can both be real and still add up to zero if they're equal and point in opposite directions.
